note: v0.72.0 — the second counted exception to fill-empty-only. Every theme here exists in the source with a band-suffixed description (the documented content debt); this promotion replaces exactly those 500 rows with five authored sentences per theme. The normaliser refuses any other target. Track names, prefixes, codes, credentials and transfer checks are untouched.

themes.theme: The first day somebody actually remembers
themes.description: What actually happens on a first day, what to bring, and the three things worth asking before lunch.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult the three things you would want to know on your first day in a new class, and go and find one out.
bands.3–5: Write the three questions you would ask before lunch on a first day at a new school or club, and ask one of a teacher.
bands.6–8: Write a first-day plan for a new club member or a new student — where to go, whom to ask, what to bring — and have a teacher check it.
bands.9–10: Write the first-day plan you would want for a real job or placement, then run somebody else through theirs.
bands.11–12: Write and run a first-day plan for a real newcomer at a workplace or programme, and keep the record of what they asked that you had missed.

themes.theme: What the role is, said plainly
themes.description: A job description is a negotiating document; the role is what you are held to. Learning to read the gap.

bands.K–2: Say in one sentence what your job is in the classroom this week, and check it with your teacher.
bands.3–5: Write your role in a group project in two sentences and check it against what the teacher expects.
bands.6–8: Read a real job advert and write, in two sentences, what the person is actually held to; have a teacher check the gap.
bands.9–10: State your own role at a real job or placement in two sentences and check it against your manager.
bands.11–12: Write the plain-language role statement for a real position and have the manager and the person holding it both confirm it.

themes.theme: Who decides what about your work
themes.description: Who signs off what, who is consulted, and who only needs telling. The map nobody hands you.

bands.K–2: Draw who decides what in your classroom — the teacher, the helper, you — for one job you do.
bands.3–5: Draw the decision map for one school project: who signs off, who is asked, who is only told.
bands.6–8: Draw the decision map for one real task at a club, team or school and confirm it with two people involved.
bands.9–10: Draw the decision map for one real task at work and confirm it with two colleagues.
bands.11–12: Draw and confirm the decision map for a real team's recurring task, and hand it to the next newcomer as the map nobody gave you.

themes.theme: The systems you must be able to use by Friday
themes.description: The five systems that gate the work, and getting access before the access is urgent.

bands.K–2: Show an adult you can log in to the class computer or open the class app on your own.
bands.3–5: List the three school systems you need this week and show a working login for each.
bands.6–8: List every system a real project needs — accounts, tools, shared folders — and get access before it is urgent, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: List every system your first task at work needs and show a working login for each.
bands.11–12: Prepare the access list for a real newcomer's first week, get every login working before they arrive, and record what took longest.

themes.theme: Asking a question without looking incapable
themes.description: Questions that make you look careful rather than lost, and when to batch them.

bands.K–2: Save up two questions during a task and ask them together at the right moment.
bands.3–5: Write three questions before asking them, and ask all three in one go rather than one at a time.
bands.6–8: Prepare three questions for a coach or teacher, ask them in one sitting, and write down the answers so you never need to ask again.
bands.9–10: Ask three prepared questions of a manager in one sitting and record the answers usefully.
bands.11–12: Run a question batch for a real team — collected, prioritised, asked once, answered in writing — and publish the answers where the next person finds them.

themes.theme: The ninety-day mark and what should be true
themes.description: What competence looks like at ninety days, described before you get there rather than after.

bands.K–2: Say what you want to be able to do by the end of term, and tell your teacher.
bands.3–5: Write what a good term at a new school or club would look like, then check it with an adult at the end.
bands.6–8: Write your own ninety-day expectations for a new team, club or placement and have a coach or teacher correct them.
bands.9–10: Write your own ninety-day expectations for a real job and have them corrected by somebody senior.
bands.11–12: Write the ninety-day expectations for a real role you supervise or support, agree them with the person on day one, and review them together on day ninety.

themes.theme: Probation, and what it actually measures
themes.description: Probation measures reliability far more than brilliance, and the evidence is mostly ordinary.

bands.K–2: Keep a chart of the promises you made this week and whether you kept them.
bands.3–5: Keep a two-week record of things you said you would do at school and whether you did them, and show it to an adult.
bands.6–8: Keep a two-week record of commitments made and kept for a team or club, and show the pattern to a coach.
bands.9–10: Keep a two-week record of commitments made and commitments kept at work.
bands.11–12: Keep and share a two-week reliability record with a real manager, and write what a fair probation review of it would say.

themes.theme: A manager relationship that works
themes.description: A working relationship is built from predictable updates, not from being liked.

bands.K–2: Tell your teacher one thing you finished and one thing you are stuck on, at the same time each day this week.
bands.3–5: Give a teacher a short update on a project at an agreed time, with what is done and what is next.
bands.6–8: Run one check-in with a coach or teacher using an agenda you wrote, and keep the agenda for next time.
bands.9–10: Run one structured check-in with a manager using an agenda you wrote.
bands.11–12: Run four weekly check-ins with a real manager on a written agenda, and show the record of decisions they produced.

themes.theme: The colleague who shows you the real process
themes.description: The documented process and the real process differ. Finding the person who knows the second.

bands.K–2: Ask a classmate how they really do a class job, and show an adult the difference from the instructions.
bands.3–5: Find the classmate who knows how something at school really works, write it down, and check it with them.
bands.6–8: Document one real process at a club or school as it is actually done, not as the sheet says, and have the person who does it verify it.
bands.9–10: Document one real workplace process as actually performed and have it verified.
bands.11–12: Document a real process as performed, reconcile it with the written one, and get both the doer and the owner to sign the reconciled version.

themes.theme: What to do when the job is not the job advertised
themes.description: When the work is materially different from what was advertised, and what to do about it early.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult when a job you were given turned out different from what you were told, and say what changed.
bands.3–5: Write what a school role was supposed to be and what it turned out to be, and say who could fix the gap.
bands.6–8: Compare a real club, team or placement role as advertised with the role as lived, name what changed, and identify who can address it.
bands.9–10: Write the comparison for a real job, name what changed, and identify who can address it.
bands.11–12: Write the advertised-versus-actual comparison for a real role, raise it with the person who can address it, and record their answer.

themes.theme: The skill your role rests on
themes.description: Identifying the one capability the role genuinely rests on, underneath the task list.

bands.K–2: Say the one thing you are best at in class and show an adult how you know.
bands.3–5: Name the one skill a school job really depends on, and say how you would know you were getting better at it.
bands.6–8: Name the one capability a real club or team role rests on, defend the choice to a coach, and say how you would measure improvement.
bands.9–10: Name it for a real job, defend the choice, and show how you would measure improvement in it.
bands.11–12: Name the one capability a real role rests on, agree it with the person who holds the role, and set the measure you will both use.

themes.theme: Practising something while being paid to do it
themes.description: Deliberate practice inside paid work, without pretending it is not happening.

bands.K–2: Practise one skill inside a real class job every day this week and tell an adult what got easier.
bands.3–5: Build a small practice into a school task for two weeks and show what changed.
bands.6–8: Design a practice loop inside a real club or team task, run it for two weeks, and show a coach the record.
bands.9–10: Design a practice loop inside a real work task and run it for two weeks.
bands.11–12: Design and run a two-week practice loop inside real paid work, agreed with the manager, and show the measured change.

themes.theme: Learning from the person leaving
themes.description: Knowledge leaves with people. Extracting it before the last day, not on it.

bands.K–2: Ask someone who is leaving your class or club to show you one thing they know before they go.
bands.3–5: Interview a classmate who is leaving a role about how they did it, and write it up for the next person.
bands.6–8: Run a handover interview with a departing club or team member and produce something a successor could use.
bands.9–10: Run a handover interview at work and produce something a successor could use.
bands.11–12: Run a handover for a real departure, produce the document, and have the successor confirm it was enough after their first month.

themes.theme: Documentation as a skill rather than a chore
themes.description: Writing something down is a skill with technique, and it is the cheapest leverage available.

bands.K–2: Write or draw the steps of a class job so a friend can do it without asking you.
bands.3–5: Write instructions for a school task so a classmate completes it correctly without asking you.
bands.6–8: Document a real club or team task so a stranger completes it correctly without asking, and test it on somebody.
bands.9–10: Document a work task so a stranger completes it correctly without asking you.
bands.11–12: Document a real task, have two strangers follow it, and revise it from where they got stuck.

themes.theme: Getting better at the thing you avoid
themes.description: The avoided task is usually the one where the gap is largest. Approaching it deliberately.

bands.K–2: Pick the class job you like least, do the first step, and tell an adult.
bands.3–5: Pick the school task you avoid, break it into three steps, and complete the first one.
bands.6–8: Pick the avoided thing in a real club or team role, break it into three steps, and complete the first with a coach watching.
bands.9–10: Pick the avoided thing at work, break it into three steps, and complete the first.
bands.11–12: Pick the avoided task, complete all three steps on the record, and write what the gap actually was.

themes.theme: A qualification your employer will fund
themes.description: Employer-funded qualifications exist, are underused, and have a process with a deadline.

bands.K–2: Find out one thing your school will pay for that helps you learn, and ask an adult how to ask for it.
bands.3–5: Find one course or badge your school or club will fund, and find out who approves it.
bands.6–8: Find one funded course or certificate you are eligible for through a school, club or programme, identify the approver, and draft the request.
bands.9–10: Find one your employer will fund, identify the approver, and draft the request.
bands.11–12: Find an employer-funded qualification, submit the real request through the real process, and record the decision and its timing.

themes.theme: Transferable versus employer-specific
themes.description: Which of your skills you keep when the employer changes, and which evaporate at the door.

bands.K–2: Sort three things you can do into ones you could use anywhere and ones only for this classroom.
bands.3–5: Sort your school skills into ones you keep anywhere and ones that only work here, and say why.
bands.6–8: Sort the skills from a real club, team or placement into transferable and place-specific, and justify each placement to a coach.
bands.9–10: Sort your current work skills into the two lists and justify each placement.
bands.11–12: Sort a real role's skills into the two lists with the person holding it, and agree what they would keep if they left tomorrow.

themes.theme: When automation changes your task
themes.description: Automation changes the shape of a task before it removes it. Reading the change early.

bands.K–2: Find one class job a machine or app now does, and say what you do instead.
bands.3–5: Describe one school task that a computer changed, and what the person still has to do.
bands.6–8: Describe one task in a real club, team or placement that a tool has changed shape, and what it now demands of the person.
bands.9–10: Describe one task in your work that has changed shape, and what it demands now.
bands.11–12: Describe a real task's change of shape under automation, and write the new role description the manager would need.

themes.theme: Teaching the thing you just learned
themes.description: Teaching is the fastest way to find the holes in what you just learned.

bands.K–2: Teach a classmate one thing you learned this week and notice the question you could not answer.
bands.3–5: Teach one thing to a classmate and write down where their questions found a gap in what you knew.
bands.6–8: Teach one thing to a club or team member and record where their questions found gaps.
bands.9–10: Teach one thing to a colleague and record where their questions found gaps.
bands.11–12: Teach a real skill to two colleagues, record the gaps their questions found, and close them on the record.

themes.theme: Evidence of competence you keep, not the company
themes.description: Evidence of competence that lives with you rather than in an employer system.

bands.K–2: Keep one piece of work you are proud of in your own folder to show next year.
bands.3–5: Make one portfolio page of something you did at school or a club that you could show anywhere.
bands.6–8: Assemble a portfolio entry from a real club, team or placement that you could show elsewhere, with nothing private in it.
bands.9–10: Assemble a portfolio entry from real work you could show after leaving, with nothing confidential in it.
bands.11–12: Assemble and have reviewed a portfolio of real work evidence that lives with you, checked for confidentiality by the employer.

tracks.name: Safety and the line you do not cross

themes.theme: What the safety rule is protecting
themes.description: Every safety rule encodes an incident. Reading the rule back to the harm it prevents.

bands.K–2: Pick one class safety rule and say what could go wrong without it.
bands.3–5: Take three school safety rules and say what harm each one prevents.
bands.6–8: Take three rules from a real club, workshop or team and state the harm each one is protecting against, checked by a coach.
bands.9–10: Take three rules where you work and state the harm each one is protecting against.
bands.11–12: Take three real workplace rules, trace each to the incident it encodes, and present the trace to the people who must follow them.

themes.theme: Stopping work, and the right to
themes.description: The right to stop unsafe work, where it comes from, and how to use it without theatre.

bands.K–2: Practise saying 'stop, that is not safe' and telling an adult straight away.
bands.3–5: Practise the stop sentence for a school or club activity and say whom you would tell.
bands.6–8: Rehearse the stop-work sentence for a real workshop or team activity and identify who you say it to.
bands.9–10: Rehearse the stop-work sentence for a real job and identify who you say it to.
bands.11–12: Rehearse and use the stop-work sentence in a real setting, and write where the right comes from and how it was received.

themes.theme: Reporting a hazard without consequence
themes.description: Reporting routes, what protection exists, and the difference between a report and a complaint.

bands.K–2: Show an adult one thing in the classroom that could hurt someone, and say who fixes it.
bands.3–5: Find the way to report a hazard at school and say what happens after you do.
bands.6–8: Identify the hazard-reporting route at a real club, workshop or school and the protection attached to it.
bands.9–10: Identify the route where you work and the protection attached to it.
bands.11–12: Report a real hazard through the real route, follow what happens to it, and write what protection actually applied.

themes.theme: Near misses and why they are the data
themes.description: A near miss is the only free data a system gets. Why they go unreported and how to fix that.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult about one time something nearly went wrong, and what you would change.
bands.3–5: Write down one near miss at school or a club and say what it tells you.
bands.6–8: Log one near miss from a real activity properly and trace what happens to the record.
bands.9–10: Log one near miss at work properly and trace what happens to the record.
bands.11–12: Log a real near miss, trace the record to its outcome, and propose one change to how they get reported.

themes.theme: Fatigue as a safety condition
themes.description: Fatigue is a hazard with the same standing as a chemical or a height, and is treated as weakness.

bands.K–2: Notice when you are too tired to do something carefully, and say so to an adult.
bands.3–5: Keep a week's record of when you were tired at school and what was harder because of it.
bands.6–8: Map your own fatigue across a real week of school, club and sport and identify one factor you can control.
bands.9–10: Map your own fatigue risk across a real working week and identify one controllable factor.
bands.11–12: Map fatigue across a real team's week, identify the controllable factors, and raise one with the person who sets the schedule.

themes.theme: The shortcut everybody takes
themes.description: Every workplace has a normalised shortcut. Naming yours and understanding why it persists.

bands.K–2: Name one rule people skip in class and say why they skip it.
bands.3–5: Name a shortcut everyone takes at school or a club, and say what pressure causes it.
bands.6–8: Identify the normalised shortcut in a real club or workshop, describe the pressure creating it, and propose the fix to a coach.
bands.9–10: Identify the shortcut where you work, describe the pressure creating it, and propose the fix.
bands.11–12: Identify a real workplace shortcut, propose the fix to the people who take it, and record whether the pressure changed.

themes.theme: Personal protective equipment that actually fits
themes.description: Protective equipment that does not fit is not protective equipment, and fit is a right.

bands.K–2: Check that your helmet, goggles or apron fits, and tell an adult if it does not.
bands.3–5: Check that your safety equipment for sport or craft fits and say what you would do if it did not.
bands.6–8: Check the fit of your own protective equipment in a real workshop or sport against what it is for, and report the gap.
bands.9–10: Check the fit of your own equipment against its specification and report the gap.
bands.11–12: Check protective equipment fit for a real team against specification, report the gaps, and follow the replacement to its arrival.

themes.theme: An incident, and the hours after it
themes.description: The hours after an incident: preserving the scene, the record, and your own account.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult exactly what happened when something went wrong, in order, without leaving bits out.
bands.3–5: Write down what happened in an accident at school in order, as you saw it.
bands.6–8: Write the account you would need to give after a real or documented incident at a club or workshop.
bands.9–10: Write the account you would need to give, from a real or documented incident at work.
bands.11–12: Write a real incident account to the standard an investigation would accept, and preserve the record with it.

themes.theme: Speaking up about somebody else
themes.description: Raising a concern about a colleague, which is the hardest safety act and the most necessary.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult when someone is doing something unsafe, saying what you saw, not that they are bad.
bands.3–5: Practise telling an adult about a classmate's unsafe act by naming the fact, not the person.
bands.6–8: Prepare a conversation about a real teammate's unsafe act, name the fact, and separate it from the person, with a coach checking.
bands.9–10: Prepare the conversation at work, name the fact, and separate it from the person.
bands.11–12: Have the real conversation about a colleague's unsafe act, on the record, and write what changed afterwards.

themes.theme: The rule you were asked to break
themes.description: Being asked to break a rule by somebody with authority over you, and the response prepared in advance.

bands.K–2: Say what you would do if an adult told you to do something unsafe, and whom you would tell.
bands.3–5: Write what you would say if someone in charge asked you to break a safety rule, and who you would go to next.
bands.6–8: Write the response you would give if a coach or supervisor asked you to break a rule, and identify the escalation route.
bands.9–10: Write the response you would give at work, and identify the escalation route if it fails.
bands.11–12: Write and rehearse the response for a real setting, identify the escalation route, and confirm with the safety lead that it holds.

themes.theme: What your contract actually says
themes.description: Reading your own contract for the four clauses that will matter, before they matter.

bands.K–2: Find the class rules and point to the ones about time, jobs and what happens if you break them.
bands.3–5: Read a school or club agreement and find the parts about hours, duties and leaving.
bands.6–8: Locate notice, hours, duties and termination in a real club, team or part-time agreement and summarise each.
bands.9–10: Locate notice, hours, duties and termination in your own contract and summarise each.
bands.11–12: Summarise the four clauses of a real contract for somebody else, and have a union or advice service confirm the summary.

themes.theme: Hours, breaks and the law on them
themes.description: Working time, rest breaks, and the difference between what is offered and what is required.

bands.K–2: Say when your break is and why everyone needs one.
bands.3–5: Find out what breaks a young worker is entitled to and compare it to a job you know about.
bands.6–8: State the legal minimum rest and break rules for young workers where you live and compare them to a real part-time job.
bands.9–10: State the legal minimum where you are and compare it to your actual pattern.
bands.11–12: State the legal minimum, compare it to a real team's pattern, and raise a real gap with the person who sets the rota.

themes.theme: Pay: the number, the deductions, the proof
themes.description: Reading a payslip line by line, and what to do when the number is wrong.

bands.K–2: Count the money for a class shop or a chore chart and check the total with an adult.
bands.3–5: Check a worked payslip against hours and rate and find the mistake in it.
bands.6–8: Reconcile a real or worked payslip against hours worked and the stated rate, and show a checker the arithmetic.
bands.9–10: Reconcile one payslip against hours worked and the stated rate.
bands.11–12: Reconcile three months of real payslips, document any error, and take it through the correction process.

themes.theme: Raising a grievance
themes.description: A grievance is a process with steps and timescales, and it works better written than spoken.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult about something unfair, saying what happened and what you want to change.
bands.3–5: Write a short complaint about a real school problem with what happened, when, and what you want done.
bands.6–8: Draft a grievance for a real or worked example following a real club, school or team process, checked by an adult.
bands.9–10: Draft a grievance for a real or worked example, following the actual process.
bands.11–12: Draft and, where warranted, submit a real grievance following the actual process, and record each step and its timescale.

themes.theme: A union, and what one is for
themes.description: What a union is, what it can and cannot do, and how membership actually functions.

bands.K–2: Say what happens when a group of people ask for something together instead of alone.
bands.3–5: Explain to a classmate what a union is, using one real example.
bands.6–8: Explain to a coach or teacher what a union does and does not do, without slogans in either direction.
bands.9–10: Explain to somebody else what a union does, without slogans in either direction.
bands.11–12: Explain to a real group of colleagues what a union is and how membership works, and answer their questions from the rules.

themes.theme: Collective versus individual complaint
themes.description: When a problem is yours alone and when it is shared, and why that changes the route.

bands.K–2: Say whether a class problem is just yours or everyone's, and how that changes who you tell.
bands.3–5: Take one school problem and say whether it is one person's or shared, and why that matters.
bands.6–8: Take one real club or team problem and argue both framings — individual and shared — to a checker.
bands.9–10: Take one workplace problem and argue both framings.
bands.11–12: Take a real workplace problem, argue both framings to the people affected, and record which route they chose and why.

themes.theme: Discrimination and the route for it
themes.description: Discrimination, the categories protected where you are, and the specific route for it.

bands.K–2: Say what it means to be treated unfairly because of who you are, and whom you would tell.
bands.3–5: Name the groups the law protects from unfair treatment and find who at school you would go to.
bands.6–8: Identify the protected categories where you live and the route for a complaint at a real school or club.
bands.9–10: Identify the route and the time limit that applies where you work.
bands.11–12: Identify the route and time limit for a real workplace, and explain them to somebody who might need them.

themes.theme: Whistleblowing and its protections
themes.description: Disclosure in the public interest: what is protected, what is not, and the order of steps.

bands.K–2: Say what you would do if you saw something seriously wrong that an adult should know about.
bands.3–5: Write the order of people you would tell about something seriously wrong at school.
bands.6–8: Map the internal route for reporting serious wrongdoing at a real club or school and where an outside body comes in.
bands.9–10: Map the internal route and the point at which external disclosure becomes protected.
bands.11–12: Map the disclosure route for a real workplace against the law where you are, and have it checked by an advice service.

themes.theme: Redundancy, notice and what is owed
themes.description: Redundancy as a process with consultation, selection and entitlement, each contestable.

bands.K–2: Say what is fair when a class job ends early, and what the person should be told.
bands.3–5: Work out from a simple example how much notice someone should get when a job ends.
bands.6–8: Calculate the notice and payment owed in a worked example, showing the working to a checker.
bands.9–10: Calculate the notice and payment owed in a worked example.
bands.11–12: Calculate what is owed in a real or realistic case, check it against the law and the contract, and explain it to the person affected.

themes.theme: Leaving well
themes.description: Leaving without burning what you built, and what you are entitled to take.

bands.K–2: When you leave a group or job, say thank you and hand over what you were doing.
bands.3–5: Write a note handing over a school role to the next person so nothing is lost.
bands.6–8: Write a resignation and handover for a real club or team role that the coach would give a reference after.
bands.9–10: Write a resignation and handover that a former manager would give a reference after.
bands.11–12: Leave a real role with a written handover and an exit conversation, and confirm the reference that follows it.

themes.theme: The first time you supervise somebody
themes.description: The shift from doing the work to being accountable for it, and what changes on day one.

bands.K–2: When you are the leader of a game or a table, say one thing you will let others do instead of doing it yourself.
bands.3–5: Lead a small group task and write down what you stopped doing yourself so others could do it.
bands.6–8: Lead a real club or team activity and write down what you will stop doing yourself; tell the group, with a coach observing.
bands.9–10: Write down what you will stop doing yourself as a new supervisor, and tell your team.
bands.11–12: Take on real supervision of one or more people, publish what you stopped doing yourself, and review with your own manager what it cost.

themes.theme: Delegation without abandonment
themes.description: Delegating the whole task with the authority attached, and staying available without hovering.

bands.K–2: Give a friend a whole job to do in a group task and check in once without taking it back.
bands.3–5: Hand a classmate a whole piece of a project with clear instructions and an agreed time to check.
bands.6–8: Delegate one real task at a club or team with a written brief and an agreed check-in, and do not take it back.
bands.9–10: Delegate one real task at work with a written brief and an agreed check-in.
bands.11–12: Delegate a real task with authority attached, hold the check-in, and have the person say afterwards whether they were supported or abandoned.

themes.theme: A difficult conversation, prepared
themes.description: Preparing a hard conversation so that the fact leads and the judgement follows.

bands.K–2: Practise saying what happened first and how you felt second, when telling someone something hard.
bands.3–5: Write the first two sentences of a hard conversation with a classmate, fact first, and practise them.
bands.6–8: Script the opening two sentences of a real hard conversation on a team and have a coach critique them before you have it.
bands.9–10: Script the opening two sentences of a real conversation at work and have them critiqued.
bands.11–12: Prepare and hold a real difficult conversation, fact leading, and write what the judgement that followed was based on.

themes.theme: Performance, described rather than scored
themes.description: Describing performance in observable behaviour rather than a number, and why the number distorts.

bands.K–2: Say what a classmate did well using what you saw, not a mark out of ten.
bands.3–5: Rewrite a star rating for a group member as a sentence describing what they actually did.
bands.6–8: Rewrite one scored assessment from a club, team or class as a description of what was observed, checked by an adult.
bands.9–10: Rewrite one scored assessment at work as a description of what was observed.
bands.11–12: Run one real review as description rather than score, and have the person say which they found fairer and why.

themes.theme: Recruiting when you cannot pay market
themes.description: Hiring against a real constraint, and what you can offer when money is not it.

bands.K–2: Say why someone should join your team when you cannot give them a prize.
bands.3–5: Write an honest invitation to join a school club role that has no reward except the work.
bands.6–8: Write the honest pitch for a real volunteer or club role, naming what it cannot offer and what it can.
bands.9–10: Write the honest pitch for a role you would have to fill without market pay.
bands.11–12: Write and use the honest pitch for a real role, and record who applied and what they said the pitch got right.

themes.theme: Someone on your team is struggling
themes.description: Noticing that somebody is struggling, and the boundary between support and diagnosis.

bands.K–2: Notice when a classmate is having a hard time and tell a trusted adult rather than trying to fix it.
bands.3–5: Practise the question you would ask a struggling teammate, and name the adult you would go to.
bands.6–8: Rehearse the opening question for a real teammate who is struggling, and name the referral you would not attempt yourself.
bands.9–10: Rehearse the opening question at work, and name the referral you would not attempt yourself.
bands.11–12: Hold the real conversation, stay on the support side of the boundary, and record the referral you made and why.

themes.theme: Holding a gate you did not design
themes.description: Enforcing a rule you would not have written, and being honest about that with your team.

bands.K–2: Explain a class rule you did not choose to a younger child without saying it is silly.
bands.3–5: Explain a school rule you disagree with to a classmate, honestly, without pretending you wrote it.
bands.6–8: Explain one club or team rule you would not have written to the group without pretending you agree.
bands.9–10: Explain one such rule at work to your team without pretending you agree.
bands.11–12: Enforce a real rule you did not design, explain it honestly to the team, and raise your objection through the route that can change it.

themes.theme: Managing upward
themes.description: Managing your own manager: what to escalate, when, and in what form.

bands.K–2: Ask a teacher for one decision by saying what you need and by when.
bands.3–5: Write a short note to a teacher asking for a decision, with the options and what you recommend.
bands.6–8: Write one escalation to a coach or teacher for a real team problem that gives them exactly what a decision needs.
bands.9–10: Write one escalation at work that gives a decision-maker exactly what a decision needs.
bands.11–12: Send a real escalation to a real decision-maker, get the decision, and write what the note would have needed to be faster.

themes.theme: The team after somebody leaves
themes.description: A team after a departure is a different team, and pretending otherwise costs more.

bands.K–2: When someone leaves your group, say out loud who will do their job now.
bands.3–5: After a classmate leaves a project, write who takes what and tell the group.
bands.6–8: Run a redistribution conversation for a real club or team after somebody leaves and publish what changed for whom.
bands.9–10: Run a redistribution conversation at work and publish what changed for whom.
bands.11–12: Lead a real redistribution after a departure, publish it, and review four weeks later whether the load actually moved.

themes.theme: What a manager owes and does not
themes.description: The obligations of the role, and the ones people wrongly assume come with it.

bands.K–2: Say two things a group leader must do for the group and one thing they do not have to do.
bands.3–5: Write the two lists for a school club leader and check them with the teacher in charge.
bands.6–8: Write the two lists for a real coach or club leader and check them against the club's actual rules.
bands.9–10: Write the two lists for a manager and check them against your organisation's actual policy.
bands.11–12: Write the two lists for a real role you hold or support, check them against policy and law, and share them with the team.

themes.theme: The job that is done from a kitchen table
themes.description: What changes when the workplace is a room you also live in, and what does not change at all.

bands.K–2: Say what is different about doing homework at the kitchen table, and make one rule for it.
bands.3–5: Write your own rules for working at home — when, where, and when you stop.
bands.6–8: Write a working agreement for real study or club work done from home covering hours, space and availability.
bands.9–10: Write your own working agreement for a real remote job covering hours, space and availability.
bands.11–12: Write a working agreement for a real remote role, agree it with the manager, and review it after a month of use.

themes.theme: Being visible without being watched
themes.description: The difference between demonstrating work and being monitored, and where the line sits.

bands.K–2: Show an adult what you did today without them having to watch you do it.
bands.3–5: Say the difference between showing your work and being watched, using a school example.
bands.6–8: For a real online class or club platform, identify what the organisers can see and what they may not require.
bands.9–10: Identify what your employer can see and what it may not require.
bands.11–12: Identify what a real employer can see under its policy and the law, and explain the line to a colleague who was unsure.

themes.theme: A meeting that should have been three sentences
themes.description: Recognising the meeting that exists to transmit information, and the cheaper form of it.

bands.K–2: Say one class announcement in three sentences instead of a whole meeting.
bands.3–5: Turn a school group meeting into a written update and see if anything was lost.
bands.6–8: Convert one recurring club or team meeting into a written update and measure what changed, with a coach's agreement.
bands.9–10: Convert one recurring meeting at work into a written update and measure the difference.
bands.11–12: Convert a real recurring meeting, run the written form for a month, and report the time saved and anything lost.

themes.theme: Time zones and whose morning it is
themes.description: The recurring meeting time is a distribution of inconvenience, and somebody always pays it.

bands.K–2: Work out what time it is for a friend or relative far away and pick a time that is fair to both.
bands.3–5: Plan a call between two places in different time zones so neither side is always the one up early.
bands.6–8: Redesign a real online club or team schedule across time zones so the inconvenience rotates rather than settles.
bands.9–10: Redesign a schedule at work so the cost rotates rather than settles.
bands.11–12: Redesign a real distributed team's schedule with the team, and record who pays the cost each month afterwards.

themes.theme: Asking for help across a screen
themes.description: The informal channel that a corridor provides and a video call does not.

bands.K–2: Ask for help in an online class using words, because nobody can see your face.
bands.3–5: Set up one way to ask a classmate for help online that is not a big message to everyone.
bands.6–8: Establish one deliberate informal channel with a real online team or class and run it for a month.
bands.9–10: Establish one deliberate informal channel with a remote team and run it for a month.
bands.11–12: Establish and run a real informal channel for a remote team, and report after a month who used it and for what.

themes.theme: Equipment, and who pays for it
themes.description: What an employer owes for the tools of remote work, and the local position on it.

bands.K–2: List the things you need for schoolwork at home and say who got each one.
bands.3–5: List what you use for learning at home and who paid for each item.
bands.6–8: List what a real remote study or club role needs and who paid for each, and find the local rule on who should.
bands.9–10: List what you use for remote work and who paid for each item.
bands.11–12: List a real remote role's equipment, who paid, and the employer's obligation where you are, and raise any gap in writing.

themes.theme: The colleague you have never met
themes.description: Building a working relationship without shared physical space, deliberately rather than by accident.

bands.K–2: Have a proper conversation with an online classmate about something other than the work.
bands.3–5: Get to know one online classmate on purpose, with three questions you planned.
bands.6–8: Run one deliberate relationship-building conversation with a real remote teammate and write what you learned.
bands.9–10: Run one relationship-building conversation with a remote colleague.
bands.11–12: Run relationship-building conversations with every remote member of a real team and record what each one needed from you.

themes.theme: Overwork when there is no leaving time
themes.description: The commute was a boundary. Replacing it with something that also ends the day.

bands.K–2: Pick a time when homework stops every day and stick to it for a week.
bands.3–5: Design an end-of-day rule for home study and hold it for two weeks.
bands.6–8: Design an end-of-day boundary for real remote study or club work and hold it for two weeks, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design an end-of-day boundary for remote work and hold it for two weeks.
bands.11–12: Design the boundary, hold it for two weeks, and write what it took to hold it against a real team's expectations.

themes.theme: Hybrid, and who is actually in the room
themes.description: Decisions made in a room reach the people in it first, and remote colleagues last.

bands.K–2: Notice who missed a class decision because they were away, and tell them.
bands.3–5: For one class decision, write who heard it first and who heard it last.
bands.6–8: Audit one real club or team decision for who heard it when, and propose how the remote members would hear sooner.
bands.9–10: Audit one decision at work for who heard it when.
bands.11–12: Audit a month of a real hybrid team's decisions for who heard what when, and propose one change to the team.

themes.theme: Coming back, or not
themes.description: Return-to-office as a change with a process, consultation and grounds for exception.

bands.K–2: Say what changed when you went back to school in the room after learning at home.
bands.3–5: Write what a fair return to in-person learning would include for someone who found home better.
bands.6–8: Identify the process a real school or club uses for returning to in-person, and the grounds for an exception.
bands.9–10: Identify the return-to-office process where you work and the grounds for an exception.
bands.11–12: Identify the real process and exception grounds, and prepare a real or worked exception request that the process would accept.

themes.theme: The first thirty seconds
themes.description: What decides whether an interaction goes well, and how much of it is not what you say.

bands.K–2: Greet a visitor to the classroom and notice what made them smile.
bands.3–5: Practise five greetings for a school event and have a friend say which worked.
bands.6–8: Run five openings at a real club desk, stall or event and have a coach observe them.
bands.9–10: Run five openings at work and have them observed.
bands.11–12: Run and be observed on five real openings, then coach somebody else through theirs.

themes.theme: Someone angry, and not about you
themes.description: Separating the complaint from the person delivering it, and staying useful.

bands.K–2: When someone is cross about something that is not your fault, stay calm and ask what they need.
bands.3–5: Role-play a cross customer at a school stall and stay helpful without taking it personally.
bands.6–8: De-escalate a scripted complaint under observation at a club, stall or event.
bands.9–10: De-escalate a scripted complaint under observation at work.
bands.11–12: De-escalate a real complaint, on the record, and debrief with a supervisor on what separated the person from the problem.

themes.theme: What you can actually authorise
themes.description: Knowing your own limit precisely, so you neither overpromise nor refuse unnecessarily.

bands.K–2: Say what you are allowed to decide at a class stall and what you must ask an adult about.
bands.3–5: List what a helper at a school event can decide alone and what needs a teacher.
bands.6–8: State your authority limits in a real club or event role and the escalation for each, checked by the organiser.
bands.9–10: State your authority limits at work and the escalation for each.
bands.11–12: State your real authority limits, get them confirmed in writing, and use them in a live case without over- or under-promising.

themes.theme: Saying no so it can be heard
themes.description: A refusal with a reason and a next step, rather than a policy quoted at somebody.

bands.K–2: Say no to a request kindly, with a reason and one other thing the person can do.
bands.3–5: Practise three refusals for a school situation, each with a reason and a next step.
bands.6–8: Deliver three refusals with a route attached in a real club or event role.
bands.9–10: Deliver three refusals with a route attached at work.
bands.11–12: Deliver real refusals with routes attached and have a supervisor confirm the person left knowing what to do next.

themes.theme: The complaint that is a warning
themes.description: Recognising the individual complaint that is describing a systemic failure.

bands.K–2: Notice when several people say the same thing is wrong, and tell an adult it keeps happening.
bands.3–5: Spot one complaint at school that keeps coming back and say what it is really about.
bands.6–8: Identify one complaint pattern from a real club, event or stall and escalate it as a pattern to the organiser.
bands.9–10: Identify one complaint pattern at work and escalate it as a pattern.
bands.11–12: Identify a real pattern, escalate it with the evidence, and follow whether the system behind it changed.

themes.theme: Abuse, and the line you do not stand behind
themes.description: What you are not required to absorb, and the support that should exist for it.

bands.K–2: Say what you should do if someone is rude or scary to you, and whom you tell.
bands.3–5: Say what a school helper does not have to put up with and who supports them.
bands.6–8: State a real club or event's position on abuse of its helpers and what it commits to do.
bands.9–10: State your organisation's position on abuse and what it commits to.
bands.11–12: State the real policy, test it against a real or worked case, and raise any gap with the person who owns it.

themes.theme: A vulnerable customer
themes.description: Recognising when the ordinary process will fail somebody, and what to do instead.

bands.K–2: Notice when someone needs extra help and get an adult rather than rushing them.
bands.3–5: Say the signs that someone at a school event needs a different kind of help, and what you would do.
bands.6–8: Identify the flags and the alternative route for a vulnerable person at a real club, event or stall.
bands.9–10: Identify the flags and the alternative route at work.
bands.11–12: Identify the flags and route in a real setting, use them in a live case, and record what the ordinary process would have missed.

themes.theme: Recording an interaction fairly
themes.description: Notes that are accurate about what happened rather than protective of who wrote them.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult what happened in a disagreement using only what was said and done.
bands.3–5: Write a fair record of a school disagreement that both people would agree is true.
bands.6–8: Write a record of a real difficult interaction at a club or event and have it reviewed for fairness.
bands.9–10: Write a record of a difficult interaction at work and have it reviewed.
bands.11–12: Write real records for a month and have a supervisor review them for accuracy rather than self-protection.

themes.theme: The handover to somebody else
themes.description: Passing a live problem without the customer having to start again.

bands.K–2: When you pass a job to a friend, tell them what has already been done so they do not start again.
bands.3–5: Hand over a school helper task to a classmate with a short written summary.
bands.6–8: Run one real handover of a live problem at a club or event with a written summary, so the person does not start again.
bands.9–10: Run one handover at work with a written summary.
bands.11–12: Run real handovers for a week and have the receivers confirm no customer had to start again.

themes.theme: Repairing it afterwards
themes.description: What follow-up actually changes, and the cases where an apology is the whole remedy.

bands.K–2: After something went wrong for someone, say sorry properly and do one thing to make it better.
bands.3–5: Plan a follow-up for a school event that went badly for someone, including the apology.
bands.6–8: Design a follow-up for one real failed interaction at a club or event, and carry it out with the organiser.
bands.9–10: Design a follow-up for one failed interaction at work.
bands.11–12: Design and deliver the follow-up for a real failure, and record whether the apology or the action was the remedy.

themes.theme: What you are actually being asked to do
themes.description: Separating the stated job from the accumulated one, in writing.

bands.K–2: List every job you do in class this week and circle the ones that are really yours.
bands.3–5: List everything you do for a school role and mark what was actually asked of you.
bands.6–8: List everything you do in a real club, team or part-time role and mark what is in the role as described, with a checker.
bands.9–10: List everything you do at work and mark what is in your role description.
bands.11–12: List a real role's accumulated work against its description and agree with the manager which items stay.

themes.theme: A workload that does not fit the hours
themes.description: Describing overload as arithmetic rather than as a personal difficulty.

bands.K–2: Add up how long your homework takes and show an adult if it is more than the time you have.
bands.3–5: Add up the hours a week of school work actually takes and compare it to the time available.
bands.6–8: Produce the hours arithmetic for a real week of school, club and part-time work, and show a checker where it does not fit.
bands.9–10: Produce the hours arithmetic for your own workload.
bands.11–12: Produce the hours arithmetic for a real team and present it as arithmetic, not difficulty, to the person who can change it.

themes.theme: Prioritising when everything is urgent
themes.description: A method for deciding, and being able to show the method to whoever disagrees.

bands.K–2: When you have three jobs, put them in order and say why to an adult.
bands.3–5: Order a real list of school tasks with a method you can explain to a classmate.
bands.6–8: Apply one prioritisation method to a real backlog of club or school tasks and defend it to a coach.
bands.9–10: Apply one prioritisation method to a real backlog at work and defend it.
bands.11–12: Apply a method to a real team backlog, publish the order and the method, and defend it to whoever disagrees.

themes.theme: Saying that something will not be done
themes.description: Making the trade-off visible to the person who owns it rather than absorbing it silently.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult which job you cannot finish today, rather than leaving it quietly.
bands.3–5: Write a note saying which school task will not be done and what you did instead.
bands.6–8: Deliver one trade-off in writing to a coach or teacher for a real club or school task.
bands.9–10: Deliver one trade-off to a decision-maker at work in writing.
bands.11–12: Deliver real trade-offs in writing for a month and record which the decision-maker accepted and which they overrode.

themes.theme: Interruption as a workload item
themes.description: Counting what is not on the list, because it is most of the day.

bands.K–2: Count how many times you were interrupted during one task and tell an adult.
bands.3–5: Keep a tally of interruptions during a week of homework and add up the time.
bands.6–8: Log interruptions for a week of real study, club or part-time work and quantify them for a checker.
bands.9–10: Log interruptions at work for a week and quantify them.
bands.11–12: Log a real team's interruptions for a week, quantify them, and propose one change to the person who can make it.

themes.theme: Deadlines you did not set
themes.description: Testing whether a deadline is real, and what happens on the day after it.

bands.K–2: Ask what happens if a class deadline is missed, and whether it could move.
bands.3–5: Test whether a school deadline is real by asking what happens the day after.
bands.6–8: Test three real deadlines from clubs, school or part-time work and record which were negotiable.
bands.9–10: Test three deadlines at work and record which were negotiable.
bands.11–12: Test three real deadlines by asking their owners what the day after holds, and publish which were real.

themes.theme: The task that expands to fill everything
themes.description: Recognising and bounding the work that has no natural end.

bands.K–2: Decide what 'finished' means for a drawing or a build before you start, and stop there.
bands.3–5: Write what 'enough' means for one school project before starting, and stop at it.
bands.6–8: Bound one real open-ended club or school task with a definition of enough, agreed with a checker.
bands.9–10: Bound one open-ended task at work with a definition of enough.
bands.11–12: Bound a real open-ended task with a written definition of enough, agree it with the owner, and hold to it.

themes.theme: Leave, and actually taking it
themes.description: Entitlement, the practical obstacles, and the cover that makes it possible.

bands.K–2: Say why everyone needs days off and what has to be ready before you take one.
bands.3–5: Plan a day away from a school role including who covers your job.
bands.6–8: Plan real time off from a club or team role including the cover arrangement, and take it.
bands.9–10: Plan leave from work including the cover arrangement.
bands.11–12: Plan and take real leave with the cover arrangement written, and record whether the cover held.

themes.theme: Being on call
themes.description: What on-call costs, what it should pay, and the rest that must follow it.

bands.K–2: Say what it is like to have to be ready to help at any time, and why you need rest after.
bands.3–5: Describe what being on call would cost someone and what rest they should get.
bands.6–8: State the on-call terms of a real role you know — a lifeguard, a first-aider, a coach — and the recovery attached.
bands.9–10: State your own on-call terms and the recovery attached.
bands.11–12: State the real on-call terms for a role, check them against law and policy, and raise any gap in writing.

themes.theme: The month you cannot sustain
themes.description: Recognising an unsustainable period in advance and naming it before it ends badly.

bands.K–2: Say how you know when you are doing too much, and tell an adult.
bands.3–5: Write the signs that a school term is getting too heavy, and what you would do about them.
bands.6–8: Write the early-warning signs of an unsustainable period across school, club and work, and show a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the early-warning signs you would act on at work.
bands.11–12: Write the signs, agree with a manager what happens when they appear, and use them once in a real period.

themes.theme: The announcement, and what it did not say
themes.description: Reading a restructure announcement for what is decided and what is still open.

bands.K–2: Listen to a class announcement and say what has been decided and what has not.
bands.3–5: Read a school announcement and sort it into decided and still open.
bands.6–8: Analyse one real announcement from a school, club or organisation for decided and undecided, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Analyse one real workplace announcement for decided and undecided.
bands.11–12: Analyse a real restructure announcement for decided and undecided, and put the open questions to the person who issued it.

themes.theme: Consultation, and whether it is real
themes.description: The difference between being consulted and being informed, and how to tell.

bands.K–2: Say the difference between being asked what you think and being told what will happen.
bands.3–5: Give two ways to tell whether a school is really asking your opinion or just informing you.
bands.6–8: Identify three tests for real consultation and apply them to a real school or club decision.
bands.9–10: Identify three tests and apply them to a real consultation process at work.
bands.11–12: Apply the tests to a real consultation, document the result, and raise it through the route that can respond.

themes.theme: A merger and the two ways of doing everything
themes.description: What happens when two sets of practice meet, and who is expected to change.

bands.K–2: When two groups join, say which way of doing something each group had and pick one fairly.
bands.3–5: Describe one thing two merged classes or clubs did differently, and how they chose.
bands.6–8: Map one process under both approaches when two real clubs, teams or classes merge, and say who was expected to change.
bands.9–10: Map one process under both approaches in a real merger.
bands.11–12: Map a real merged process under both approaches with people from both sides, and record who changed and why.

themes.theme: New ownership
themes.description: What transfers with a business sale and what your position is on the day after.

bands.K–2: Say what stays the same and what might change when a shop or club gets a new owner.
bands.3–5: List what would change for the staff if a local shop was sold.
bands.6–8: State what transfers with a business sale where you live, using a real local example.
bands.9–10: State what transfers with a business sale where you are.
bands.11–12: State what transfers for a real or realistic sale, check it against the law, and explain it to somebody affected.

themes.theme: A closure with a date on it
themes.description: The sequence, the entitlements, and the things that must be done before the last day.

bands.K–2: Make a list of what has to happen before a class project or club ends on its last day.
bands.3–5: Build the checklist for closing down a school club properly, with dates.
bands.6–8: Build the closure checklist for a real club, team or event role with a date on it.
bands.9–10: Build the closure checklist for your own role in a real closure.
bands.11–12: Build and run the closure checklist for a real role, and record what the entitlements and last-day duties actually were.

themes.theme: Selection, and the criteria used
themes.description: How selection for redundancy is supposed to work, and what makes it contestable.

bands.K–2: Say how a team was picked and whether the way was fair.
bands.3–5: Read the rules for picking a school team and find one that could be unfair.
bands.6–8: Read one real selection matrix from a school, club or programme and identify a contestable element.
bands.9–10: Read one selection matrix at work and identify a contestable element.
bands.11–12: Read a real selection matrix, identify the contestable element, and set out how it would be contested.

themes.theme: The colleague who is going
themes.description: Behaving well toward somebody whose outcome differed from yours.

bands.K–2: Be kind to a classmate who did not get picked, and say what you would do in their first week.
bands.3–5: Describe what you would do in the first week for a friend who lost a school role you kept.
bands.6–8: Describe what you would do in the first week for a real teammate whose outcome differed from yours.
bands.9–10: Describe what you would do in the first week at work.
bands.11–12: Do it, in a real case, and write what behaving well actually required.

themes.theme: Surviving a restructure and the guilt after
themes.description: The known effect on the people who stay, and what teams do about it.

bands.K–2: Say how the people who stay feel when friends leave a group, and what would help.
bands.3–5: Say what a class needs after several classmates leave, and plan one thing.
bands.6–8: Identify what a real club or team would need after a round of departures, and propose it to the coach.
bands.9–10: Identify what your team at work would need afterwards.
bands.11–12: Identify what a real team needed after a restructure, provide one part of it, and record whether it helped.

themes.theme: A reference, requested and given
themes.description: What a reference may say, what it may not, and what to ask for while you can.

bands.K–2: Ask a teacher to say one true thing about your work that you could show someone else.
bands.3–5: Ask an adult for a short written reference for a school role and check it says what you need.
bands.6–8: Request one reference from a real coach, teacher or employer and check what it commits to.
bands.9–10: Request one reference at work and check what it commits to.
bands.11–12: Request a real reference, check it against what a reference may and may not say, and give one properly for somebody else.

themes.theme: Rebuilding after
themes.description: What the new organisation actually is, versus the one described in the announcement.

bands.K–2: Say what a class is really like after a big change, compared to what you were told.
bands.3–5: Compare what a school change was supposed to be with what it turned out to be after a term.
bands.6–8: Compare a real described change at a club or school to the real one after ninety days, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compare the described change at work to the real one after ninety days.
bands.11–12: Compare a real described change to the real one at ninety days, and present the comparison to the people who announced it.

themes.theme: The first ten years and what they are for
themes.description: Treating early work as accumulation of evidence rather than a ladder.

bands.K–2: Say three things you want to be able to do by the end of primary school.
bands.3–5: Write what your first years at secondary school should produce, specifically.
bands.6–8: Write what your first years of work or study should produce as evidence, specifically, and check it with an adult who has done it.
bands.9–10: Write what your first years of work should produce, specifically.
bands.11–12: Write the evidence your first years should produce, review it with somebody ten years ahead, and revise it on the record.

themes.theme: A sideways move that is not a demotion
themes.description: When breadth beats a title, and how to explain the choice later.

bands.K–2: Say why trying a different job in class can be better than being the boss of the same one.
bands.3–5: Argue why changing to a different school role could be better than a bigger version of the same one.
bands.6–8: Argue one real sideways move — a different position on a team, a different role in a club — on its merits.
bands.9–10: Argue one sideways move at work on its merits.
bands.11–12: Make the case for a real sideways move to the person who decides it, and record the answer.

themes.theme: Money, honestly
themes.description: Knowing the market for what you do, and the specific ways people find out too late.

bands.K–2: Find out what a job you know pays and whether that seems fair.
bands.3–5: Find out from two places what a real job pays and compare them.
bands.6–8: Establish the market rate for a real part-time role from three sources and show the working.
bands.9–10: Establish the market rate for your role from three sources.
bands.11–12: Establish the market rate for a real role from three sources and use it in a real pay conversation.

themes.theme: The employer you would leave
themes.description: Deciding in advance what would make you go, so the decision is not made while exhausted.

bands.K–2: Say what would make you want to leave a club or team, before it happens.
bands.3–5: Write what would make you leave a school club, so the decision is not made when upset.
bands.6–8: Write your own conditions for leaving a real club, team or part-time job, before you need them.
bands.9–10: Write your own conditions for leaving a job.
bands.11–12: Write the conditions, review them with somebody who knows you, and test them against a real employer you have worked for.

themes.theme: Sector change
themes.description: Moving between sectors, what transfers, and what has to be re-earned.

bands.K–2: Say which of your skills would work in a completely different kind of job.
bands.3–5: Map three of your skills onto a job in a different field and say what you would have to learn.
bands.6–8: Map your real skills onto a different sector honestly, marking what transfers and what must be re-earned.
bands.9–10: Map your skills onto a different sector honestly.
bands.11–12: Map a real sector change for yourself or somebody else, with a person from the target sector checking what transfers.

themes.theme: A qualification at forty
themes.description: Returning to study around work and money, and the routes designed for it.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who learned something new as a grown-up what it took.
bands.3–5: Find one way an adult can study around work and money, and describe it.
bands.6–8: Identify one real route to a qualification for an adult around work and money, and its constraints.
bands.9–10: Identify one route that fits your actual constraints.
bands.11–12: Identify the route, the funding and the timing for a real adult learner, and help them start the application.

themes.theme: Being managed by somebody younger
themes.description: A common transition, handled badly by default and well with a little deliberateness.

bands.K–2: Say how you would treat a younger child who was put in charge of a game.
bands.3–5: Describe how you would work well with a younger classmate who leads a project.
bands.6–8: Describe how you would open a working relationship with a younger team captain or club leader, and try it.
bands.9–10: Describe how you would open that relationship at work.
bands.11–12: Open the relationship in a real case, deliberately, and write what the default would have been.

themes.theme: Work when health changes
themes.description: Adjustments, the process for requesting them, and what an employer must consider.

bands.K–2: Say what a classmate might need changed if they hurt their arm, and who arranges it.
bands.3–5: Find out how a school arranges changes for a student whose health changes.
bands.6–8: Identify the process a real school, club or employer uses for adjustments when health changes, and what it must consider.
bands.9–10: Identify the adjustments process where you are.
bands.11–12: Identify the real process, prepare a real or worked adjustment request, and check it against what the employer must consider.

themes.theme: The last decade of working
themes.description: Winding down, transferring knowledge, and the value of the person who has seen it before.

bands.K–2: Ask someone near the end of their working life what they know that nobody else does.
bands.3–5: Interview someone about the knowledge they would hand on before they stop working.
bands.6–8: Design a knowledge transfer for a role a departing adult holds, and run one session of it.
bands.9–10: Design a knowledge transfer for a role you hold.
bands.11–12: Design and run a knowledge transfer for a real role nearing its end, and have the receiver confirm what was captured.

themes.theme: Stopping
themes.description: Retirement, phased or otherwise, and the identity question underneath the financial one.

bands.K–2: Say what a grown-up might do with their time when they stop working.
bands.3–5: Write what you think the first year of retirement should hold, and ask a retired person.
bands.6–8: Interview a retired person about their first year, and write what the identity question underneath the money one was.
bands.9–10: Write what you would do with the first year of retirement.
bands.11–12: Write the first-year plan for a real person approaching retirement, with them, covering money and identity separately.
